title: Calcium Carbonate (Food Grade)
description: Food-grade calcium supplement and pH regulator for food products.

details.longDescription:
Calcium carbonate (CaCO3, CAS 471-34-1) is the food additive E170. It is supplied here as food grade: a fine white powder of 98–100% CaCO3, about 40% calcium, in 25 kg bags, for flour millers, bakeries, makers of breakfast cereals, plant-based drinks, confectionery and chewing gum, beverage producers and supplement manufacturers.

Its main food use is as a calcium source. At about 40% calcium by weight it is among the most concentrated calcium salts, and it is used to fortify flour, bread, breakfast cereals and plant-based milks; in the United Kingdom, for example, calcium carbonate must by law be added to most wheat flour other than wholemeal. It is also used as an acidity regulator and anti-caking agent in powdered foods, as a white colour (E170 is listed as a colour in the EU), as a filler in chewing gum base, and to deacidify wine and fruit juices, where it neutralises tartaric and other acids. The specification gives 0.1–2% as the typical dosage in foods, and 8–10 as the pH of a 10% slurry.

Food-grade calcium carbonate is made either by precipitation (precipitated calcium carbonate, PCC), which gives a fine, even powder (the specification here gives 2–10 microns for the precipitated grade), or by grinding pure limestone or marble (ground calcium carbonate). Confirm the form and particle size you need when ordering, because fineness affects mouthfeel, suspension in drinks and dispersion in flour. The site also lists calcium carbonate in an industrial grade, ground and precipitated, for construction, plastics and paints, and a water-treatment grade of 95–98% at 200–325 mesh for pH and alkalinity correction. This listing is the food grade; what sets it apart is the impurity limits that apply to a food additive, such as lead, arsenic and other heavy metals, fluoride and acid-insoluble matter, and the documents that go with them.

Handling and storage: calcium carbonate is not classified as hazardous under GHS by most suppliers and is not regulated for transport. Fine powder raises dust that irritates the eyes and airways, so use dust extraction or wear a dust mask and goggles when emptying bags. It reacts with acids, releasing carbon dioxide that can foam over or pressurise a closed vessel, so add it slowly when deacidifying. Keep bags closed, dry and off the floor, since damp powder lumps and flows poorly, and store food-grade stock away from acids and from non-food chemicals.

It is packed in 25 kg bags and comes with a safety data sheet, with same-day delivery in Muscat, next-day dispatch to Sohar, two to three days to Salalah, and export across the GCC. It is supplied as food grade; ask for the specification and certificate of analysis with your quote, stating form, particle size and quantity.

title: Calcium Lactate (Food Grade)
description: Calcium fortification agent and firming agent for food processing.

details.longDescription:
Calcium lactate (E327) is the calcium salt of lactic acid, supplied by Global Chemicals LLC as the pentahydrate (C6H10CaO6·5H2O, CAS 5743-47-5), a white crystalline powder with about 13% calcium, readily soluble in water and neutral in taste, in 25 kg bags and drums from stock in Muscat. It meets the E327 specification and the US FDA GRAS listing, and every lot ships with a certificate of analysis and food-grade documentation.

Why food processors choose it. Calcium lactate dissolves completely and tastes clean, which is why it fortifies clear beverages, juices, sports and electrolyte drinks and flavoured waters where calcium carbonate would settle and leave a chalky mouthfeel; typical use runs 0.2–0.5% of the beverage, up to about 1% for high-calcium claims, within the salt's solubility of roughly 5–9 g per 100 mL. It is well absorbed, so it is also a calcium source in dairy enrichment, nutritional supplements and pharmaceutical calcium tablets.

As a firming agent it keeps canned and frozen fruit and vegetables, pickles and pre-cut fresh produce crisp: calcium ions cross-link pectin in the plant cell walls, so slices and pieces hold their shape through heat processing; dips of 0.5–1% are typical for fresh-cut fruit. In jams, jellies and low-sugar fruit preparations it supplies the calcium that sets low-methoxyl pectin and alginate gels, and in baking it is a component of some leavening systems and a dough improver.

Formulation notes: calcium lactate is compatible with most acids and flavours but will precipitate with phosphates, carbonates and sulphates at high concentrations, so add it after other salts and check clarity in a bench trial. It is also the calcium source in spherification with sodium alginate. The pentahydrate loses water if stored warm and dry, so keep bags closed and below 30 °C; it is non-hazardous.

title: Citric Acid Anhydrous (Food Grade)
description: Food-grade acidulant and preservative for flavoring and pH control.

details.longDescription:
Citric acid anhydrous (C6H8O7, CAS 77-92-9) is the water-free form of citric acid, the food additive E330. It is supplied here as food grade: white crystalline granules or free-flowing powder of 99.5% minimum purity, in 25 kg bags or cartons, for soft-drink and juice plants, confectioners, jam and sauce makers, dairies, canneries and other food manufacturers.

It is the main acid in fruit drinks, lemon-lime sodas and many sports drinks (colas use phosphoric acid), where it gives the sour taste and lowers the pH so that preservatives such as sodium benzoate and potassium sorbate work. Typical use in foods is 0.1–1.5%. A 1% solution has a pH of about 2.2 and a 0.1 M solution about 2.1. In jams and jellies it brings the pH into the range of about 2.8–3.5 that high-methoxyl pectin needs to set; in canned fruit and vegetables it is used to bring the product to pH 4.6 or below, the limit above which Clostridium botulinum can grow; it is the sour coating on sour sweets; and with sodium bicarbonate it is the acid in effervescent powders and tablets.

It also binds metal ions. That chelating action slows metal-catalysed oxidation in oils, fats and seafood, which is why it is described as an antioxidant synergist rather than an antioxidant in its own right, and together with ascorbic acid it slows enzymatic browning of cut fruit and vegetables. In cheese making it acidifies milk for direct-acid mozzarella and coagulates hot milk for paneer, and in food plants it is used to descale equipment. The anhydrous form carries no water of crystallisation; the site's citric acid monohydrate (CAS 5949-29-1) carries about 8.6%, so 1.094 kg of monohydrate supplies the same acid as 1 kg of anhydrous, and recipes should state which form they mean. The site also lists liquid citric acid for RO membrane cleaning and for oilfield acidising; this listing is the food grade.

Handling and storage: citric acid causes serious eye irritation (H319) and is not regulated for transport. Wear goggles and gloves, and a dust mask when emptying bags; fine dust is combustible. It reacts with carbonates and bicarbonates to release carbon dioxide and with strong bases to release heat, and its solutions corrode carbon steel, zinc, copper and brass, so use stainless steel or plastic for solutions. The anhydrous powder picks up moisture and cakes in humid storage: keep bags closed, dry, off the floor and away from bases, oxidisers and nitrates, and store food-grade stock apart from industrial chemicals.

It is packed in 25 kg bags or cartons. It is supplied as food grade; ask for the specification (E330, FCC or JECFA) and the lot certificate of analysis with your quote, stating quantity and pack size.
technicalSpecs: Food additive E330; FCC/JECFA specification on request

faqs.question: What is the difference between food-grade and technical-grade citric acid?
faqs.answer: Food-grade citric acid is made to food-additive specifications such as JECFA (Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives), the EU E330 specification and FCC (Food Chemicals Codex); pharmaceutical grades follow the pharmacopoeias (BP/EP, USP). These set upper limits on lead (0.5 mg/kg) and other heavy metals, oxalate, sulphated ash and readily carbonisable substances. Technical-grade citric acid (also called industrial-grade) is manufactured to lower purity standards at reduced cost and may contain higher levels of heavy metal impurities and microbial contamination. Technical-grade citric acid must never be used in food or pharmaceutical production as the impurity profile is not controlled to a level safe for human consumption. title: Ethanol 70% (Food Grade)
description: Food-grade ethanol for sanitization and extraction processes.

details.longDescription:
Ethanol 70% (ethyl alcohol, C2H5OH, CAS 64-17-5) is a ready-to-use blend of 70% v/v ethanol in water, supplied as food grade, for sanitising food-contact surfaces, equipment and hands in food and beverage plants, commercial kitchens, catering and laboratories, and for preparing herbal and flavour extracts.

Ethanol kills vegetative bacteria, yeasts, moulds and enveloped viruses by denaturing proteins and disrupting cell membranes. It works best between roughly 60% and 90% v/v: the water in the blend slows evaporation and helps the alcohol penetrate cells, so 70% acts better on most bacteria than absolute ethanol, which coagulates the outer proteins and evaporates before it has done its work. It has little effect on bacterial spores and acts more slowly on some non-enveloped viruses such as norovirus. It is a sanitiser, not a cleaner: soil and grease must be removed first, and the surface has to stay visibly wet for the contact time set by the site's hygiene procedure. On clean, dry surfaces it evaporates without leaving a residue, which is why it is used on equipment and food-contact areas that should not stay wet with water, and on small parts and utensils between production runs; whether a rinse is needed is set by the site's food-safety plan and local rules.

As an extraction solvent, a 70% water–alcohol mix draws both water-soluble and alcohol-soluble compounds from herbs, spices and botanicals, which makes it a common strength for tinctures and flavour extracts. Essential oils, by contrast, are normally recovered by steam distillation or pressing, and less polar extracts need higher-strength ethanol; the absolute laboratory grade and the industrial grade are listed separately on this site. Use the 70% blend where the water content is wanted, not where a dry solvent is required.

Handling and storage: ethanol 70% is still a highly flammable liquid and vapour, with a flash point below normal room temperature, and causes serious eye irritation (H225, H319). It travels as Class 3 dangerous goods, UN 1170. Keep containers closed in a cool, ventilated area away from sparks, open flames, hot surfaces and oxidisers such as hypochlorite, peroxides and nitric acid; do not spray it onto hot equipment or near burners; earth containers when decanting from 200 L drums; and wear safety glasses, with gloves for repeated use. Wiping or spraying large areas gives off vapour, so ventilate the room.

It is supplied in 5 L, 20 L and 200 L packs with a certificate of analysis and safety data sheet, with same-day delivery within Muscat and road delivery across the GCC. It is supplied as food grade; ask for the specification and supporting documents with your quote, stating pack size and volume.

title: Formaldehyde 40% (Technical Grade)
description: Industrial disinfectant, fumigant and preservative for empty facilities and non-food-contact equipment.

details.longDescription:
Formaldehyde 40%, sold as formalin, is a 37–40% solution of formaldehyde (CH2O, CAS 50-00-0) in water stabilised with 10–15% methanol to stop it polymerising into paraformaldehyde. Global Chemicals LLC supplies the technical grade in 30 L containers and 200 L drums from stock in Muscat for industrial disinfection, fumigation and preservation. It is not a food-contact product: it is used to disinfect empty facilities and equipment that are then aired and rinsed before use.

Where it is used. Poultry houses and hatcheries are fumigated with formaldehyde between flocks, classically by generating the gas from formalin and potassium permanganate or by heating formalin, in a sealed, empty building that is ventilated thoroughly before birds return; cold stores, warehouses, storage tanks and vehicles are disinfected the same way. Formaldehyde kills bacteria, viruses, fungi and spores, which is why it remains in use where other disinfectants cannot reach every surface. Outside disinfection it preserves textiles, leather and biological specimens, and it is the feedstock of urea-, phenol- and melamine-formaldehyde resins.

Health and regulation. Formaldehyde is classified by IARC as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) and in the EU as a presumed carcinogen (Carc. 1B), suspected mutagen, skin sensitiser and skin-corrosive substance; it is toxic by inhalation, ingestion and skin contact, and the vapour irritates eyes and airways at very low concentrations. It must be handled only by trained staff, in well-ventilated areas or with full-face respiratory protection with formaldehyde cartridges, chemical goggles, nitrile or butyl gloves and coveralls. Fumigated buildings must be empty of people and animals and ventilated until the level falls below the workplace exposure limit before re-entry. Supply is to registered business accounts.

Storage: keep drums closed, upright, at 15–25 °C, out of sunlight and away from oxidisers, acids, alkalis and ammonia; at low temperatures (below about 5–10 °C for methanol-stabilised grades) paraformaldehyde precipitates as a white sediment, and the methanol makes the solution flammable (flash point about 50–64 °C closed cup depending on methanol content; use the value on the safety data sheet). Every delivery carries a certificate of analysis giving formaldehyde and methanol content, and a GHS safety data sheet.

Delivery is same day within Muscat and Rusayl Industrial Area, next day to Sohar, two to three days to Salalah and Duqm, and by road across the GCC with a certificate of origin. Request a quote with the pack size, quantity and intended use.

title: Limestone (Food Grade)
description: Food-grade calcium source and pH adjuster for food and beverage processing.

details.longDescription:
Ground limestone is natural calcium carbonate (CaCO3, CAS 471-34-1); the standard grade runs 95–98% CaCO3, giving 38–39% calcium, and material for food use (E170) must reach at least 98% CaCO3 on a dried basis, so ask for the food-grade certificate where it will reach food. It comes with low heavy metals, at least 85% whiteness and particle sizes from 50 to 200 mesh, supplied by Global Chemicals LLC in 25 kg and 50 kg bags and bulk from stock in Muscat. A 10% slurry reads about pH 9, so it neutralises acidity gently and without the overshoot of lime or caustic.

Food, feed and agriculture. Feed mills use it as the main calcium source in poultry and livestock rations: layer hens need coarse particles of 2–4 mm for strong eggshells, a different size from the 50–200 mesh powder listed here, so specify the layer grade when ordering; broiler and ruminant feeds take the fine grades. Food processors use it as a calcium fortificant and acidity regulator (E170) and as a neutralising agent for acidic process streams and wastes. Beet sugar factories and sugar refineries burn limestone to make the quicklime and carbon dioxide used to purify juice by carbonatation. In agriculture it is the standard liming material for acidic soils and growing media, and a calcium source where gypsum is not wanted.

Industrial uses. Water-treatment plants use limestone contactors and dosing to remineralise and stabilise desalinated water, and to neutralise acidic effluent; flue-gas desulphurisation scrubbers use limestone slurry to capture sulphur dioxide; and construction uses the coarser grades as filler and aggregate. For high-brightness industrial grades in plastics, paint and paper, see the calcium carbonate page.

Choosing the grade: ask for food or feed grade where the product will reach food or animal feed, and specify the particle size for the job, because reaction speed and handling depend on fineness. The powder is non-hazardous; avoid breathing dust, wear a dust mask when tipping bags, and keep bags dry, as damp limestone cakes and flows poorly. Every lot carries a certificate of analysis giving CaCO3 content, particle size, moisture and heavy metals, and a safety data sheet.

title: Caustic Soda Liquid (Food Grade)
description: Food-grade alkali for cleaning and pH adjustment in food processing.

details.longDescription:
Caustic soda liquid is sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH, CAS 1310-73-2), the food additive E524. It is supplied here as food grade: a clear, colourless solution of 30–50% NaOH with low sodium chloride and iron, as shown on the certificate of analysis, and heavy metals below 5 ppm, in 25 L and 200 L containers and IBCs, for dairies, beverage and water-bottling plants, breweries, juice and fruit processors and other food manufacturers.

The largest use is clean-in-place (CIP) cleaning of tanks, pipework, heat exchangers, fillers and pasteurisers, where hot dilute caustic dissolves fat, protein and starch deposits. Working solutions are usually 0.5–2%: dairy plants commonly run 0.8–1.5% at 70–80 °C for 10–20 minutes, beverage and juice lines 0.5–1.0% at 60–75 °C, and heavily soiled fermentation vessels up to 2%. Caustic cleans but does not sanitise; a typical cycle follows it with a rinse, an acid wash to remove mineral scale and a separate sanitising step. In brewery tanks still holding carbon dioxide, caustic absorbs the gas, loses strength and can pull a vacuum on the vessel, so tanks are vented first or cleaned with acid instead. Running stronger or hotter than needed adds little and shortens the life of gaskets and seals.

In food processing itself, hot lye is used to peel produce, at about 2% for peaches and 10–20% for tomatoes and potatoes; solutions of about 2–3.5% remove the bitterness from green table olives in Spanish-style curing; a lye bath of around 3–4% gives pretzels their brown crust; and it is used to alkalise cocoa, to make some caramel colours, and for pH adjustment and neutralisation. Food grade differs from the site's industrial caustic soda liquid for water treatment (32%, 48% or 50%) and soap making (30%, 48% or 50%) in its impurity limits and documents, not in the chemical. Flakes, prills and liquid are compared in the caustic soda guide linked on this page.

Handling and storage: sodium hydroxide solution may be corrosive to metals and causes severe skin burns and eye damage (H290, H314), and travels as Class 8 dangerous goods, UN 1824. Even dilute CIP solutions can cause permanent eye damage, so wear chemical-resistant gloves, goggles and a face shield and keep an eyewash station nearby. Diluting releases heat: add caustic slowly to water with stirring, never water to caustic. Keep it away from acids, from aluminium, zinc, tin and galvanised fittings, which it attacks with release of hydrogen, and from ammonium salts, which release ammonia. Store it in closed steel or HDPE containers; 50% solution starts to crystallise below about 12 °C.

It is supplied in 25 L and 200 L containers and IBCs, with a certificate of analysis. It is supplied as food grade; ask for the specification and food-grade documents with your quote, stating concentration, pack size and volume.

It is also used in food processing itself: for pretzel crust formation (lye dipping), olive curing, noodle making, and pH adjustment in beverages. In Oman's food manufacturing sector, food-grade caustic soda is essential for dairy processing, juicing plants, water bottling lines, and fish processing CIP programmes. title: Potassium Sorbate (Food Grade)
description: Preservative for preventing mold and yeast growth in food and beverages.

details.longDescription:
Potassium sorbate (the potassium salt of sorbic acid, C6H7KO2, CAS 24634-61-5) is the food additive E202; sorbic acid itself is E200. It is supplied here as food grade: a white crystalline powder or granules of 99% minimum purity, in 25 kg bags or cartons, for juice and soft-drink bottlers, bakeries, dairies and cheese makers, and makers of sauces, dressings, spreads, pickles and dried fruit.

It inhibits moulds and yeasts and is much weaker against most bacteria, so it extends shelf life but does not replace heat treatment, acidity or hygiene. The active form is undissociated sorbic acid (pKa 4.76), so it works best in acidic foods and loses most of its effect above about pH 6.5. Typical use is 0.025–0.1% expressed as sorbic acid, within the limits your local food-additive regulations set for each food; 1.34 g of potassium sorbate supplies 1 g of sorbic acid. It dissolves readily, about 58 g in 100 mL of water at 20 °C, which is why it is used in place of sorbic acid in drinks, syrups, brines and dipping solutions, and it is practically odourless with a neutral taste at normal use levels.

The main uses are fruit juices, soft drinks and syrups; cheese, in the product or in surface treatments and coatings; sauces, dressings, margarine and spreads; pickles; and dried fruit. Because it also inhibits baker's yeast, it is not added to yeast-raised dough in quantity: bread is sprayed on the surface after baking or preserved with calcium propionate instead, while cakes and other chemically leavened goods take it in the mix. In wine it is added at bottling to stop sweetened wine refermenting in the bottle, but it does not stop an active fermentation and it must be used with sulphur dioxide, because lactic acid bacteria can turn sorbate into a compound with a strong geranium-like off-odour. In acidic soft drinks it is often used together with sodium benzoate; total preservative levels are set per product.

Handling and storage: many suppliers classify potassium sorbate as a skin and eye irritant (H315, H319; some also H335 for dust), and it is not regulated for transport. Wear goggles, gloves and a dust mask when emptying bags, and keep dust away from ignition sources, as fine dust clouds are combustible. It slowly oxidises and yellows when exposed to air, light, heat and moisture, so keep bags closed in a cool, dry, dark store, off the floor and away from strong oxidising agents, and use stock in rotation. Store food-grade stock apart from industrial chemicals.

It is held in stock in Muscat and packed in 25 kg bags or cartons. It is supplied as food grade; ask for the specification and certificate of analysis with your quote, stating quantity and pack size.

title: Sodium Bicarbonate (Food Grade)
description: Food-grade baking soda for leavening, pH control, and food processing.

details.longDescription:
Sodium bicarbonate (baking soda, sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO3, CAS 144-55-8) is the food additive E500(ii). It is supplied here as food grade: a fine white crystalline powder of 99.5% minimum purity in 25 kg and 50 kg bags, for bakeries, biscuit and snack makers, beverage plants, dairies and other food manufacturers.

Its main use is leavening. Heated on its own it gives off carbon dioxide slowly and leaves sodium carbonate, which tastes soapy and turns baked goods yellow, so it is normally paired with an acid: buttermilk, yoghurt, citric acid, or leavening acids such as sodium acid pyrophosphate and monocalcium phosphate. The acid releases carbon dioxide that raises cakes, biscuits, crackers, quick breads and batters, and baking powder is simply sodium bicarbonate blended with one or more of these acids and a starch carrier. The typical dosage in baking given in the specification is 0.5–3%, depending on the product and the acid used.

Outside baking it is a mild alkali and buffer: a 0.1 M solution has a pH of about 8.3, and about 9.6 g dissolves in 100 mL of water at 20 °C. It is used to adjust and buffer pH in soft drinks and mineral waters, as the carbon dioxide source in effervescent drink powders and tablets made with citric acid, to control acidity in some dairy processing, to tenderise meat and to keep green vegetables green during cooking, although too much softens them and destroys some vitamins, notably thiamine and vitamin C. Dilute solutions are also used to clean and deodorise food-plant surfaces. The site also lists sodium bicarbonate for water treatment, 99% minimum, dosed to raise alkalinity and buffer pH; this listing is the food grade.

Handling and storage: sodium bicarbonate is not classified as hazardous under GHS by most suppliers and is not regulated for transport. Dust can irritate the eyes, so wear goggles and a dust mask when emptying bags in quantity. It reacts with acids to release carbon dioxide, which can pressurise closed containers, and it starts to break down to sodium carbonate above about 50 °C, so keep bags closed, dry, off the floor and away from acids and heat, and use stock in rotation; damp bicarbonate cakes and loses leavening power. Store food-grade stock apart from industrial chemicals.

It is packed in 25 kg and 50 kg bags. It is supplied as food grade; ask for the specification and certificate of analysis with your quote, stating quantity and pack size.

title: Sodium Hypochlorite (Food Grade)
description: Food-grade sanitizing agent for food contact surfaces and equipment.

details.longDescription:
Sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl, CAS 7681-52-9) is a widely used chlorine sanitiser in the food industry: a pale yellow-green alkaline solution, pH 11–13, containing 5–12.5% available chlorine, supplied as food grade for sanitising food-contact surfaces, equipment, utensils and produce wash water in food plants, commercial kitchens, poultry, meat and fish processing, and fruit and vegetable packing.

It is used diluted. On cleaned food-contact surfaces and equipment the usual range is 50–200 ppm available chlorine with a contact time of 1–2 minutes; 200 ppm is about 2 mL of a 10% solution per litre of water, or 1.6 mL of a 12.5% solution. Produce wash water is typically held at 50–200 ppm, commonly 100–150 ppm, with the pH at 6.5–7.5, where half or more of the free chlorine is the fast-acting hypochlorous acid (HOCl); at pH 8 only about a quarter is HOCl and the wash works much more slowly. Organic soil consumes chlorine, so surfaces must be cleaned before sanitising, and wash water checked with test strips or a photometer and topped up. Going above the working range adds little and increases corrosion of stainless steel and the risk of off-flavours.

Whether a rinse is needed after sanitising is set by local food-safety rules. In the United States, for example, a sodium hypochlorite sanitising solution may be left on food-contact surfaces without a potable-water rinse only up to 200 ppm available chlorine (21 CFR 178.1010), and produce washed in chlorinated water is normally given a potable-water rinse. In Oman, follow the requirements of the food-safety authority and your HACCP plan. Food-grade sodium hypochlorite differs from industrial and pool grades in the documentation and impurity limits that go with it, not in the active chemical, and scented or thickened household bleach should never be used on food-contact surfaces. Other grades and strengths are covered in the sodium hypochlorite guide linked on this page.

Handling and storage: sodium hypochlorite solution causes severe skin burns and eye damage and is very toxic to aquatic life (H314 and H400, with H410 or H411 according to the supplier's safety data sheet), and contact with acids liberates toxic gas (EUH031). It travels as Class 8 dangerous goods, UN 1791. Never mix it with acids, acidic cleaners or descalers, which release chlorine gas, or with ammonia or ammonium compounds, which form chloramines. It loses strength with heat, sunlight and time, faster in an Omani summer, so store it upright in its original container, closed, shaded and cool, away from metals such as copper and nickel, and use stock in rotation. Wear chemical-resistant gloves and goggles or a face shield when handling the concentrate.

It is supplied in 25 L, 60 L and 200 L containers. It is supplied as food grade; ask for the specification and concentration certificate with your quote, stating strength, pack size and volume.
applications: Cutting board and prep surface sanitizing
technicalSpecs: Hazard: H314, H400, EUH031 — UN 1791, Class 8

faqs.question: What is food-grade sodium hypochlorite and how is it used in food processing?
faqs.answer: Food-grade sodium hypochlorite is a high-purity chlorine solution produced from food-safe feedstocks, with heavy metal and impurity limits meeting food safety regulations. It is one of the most widely used disinfectants in food processing worldwide — applied as a surface sanitiser, equipment disinfectant, produce wash, and water disinfectant in CIP and COP (clean-out-of-place) programmes. At concentrations of 50–200 ppm free chlorine, it rapidly kills pathogens including Salmonella, E. coli, Listeria, and Campylobacter on contact surfaces and fresh produce. In Oman's fish processing, meat processing, vegetable packing, and catering sectors, sodium hypochlorite is used daily for sanitising work surfaces, knives, cutting boards, crates, and conveyor belts. It must be used at the correct concentration — too low is ineffective, too high risks chemical contamination and accelerates corrosion. Global Chemicals LLC supplies food-grade sodium hypochlorite with concentration certification.

faqs.question: What concentration of sodium hypochlorite is safe for fruit and vegetable washing in Oman?
faqs.answer: For fresh produce washing, the internationally recommended sodium hypochlorite concentration is 50–200 ppm free available chlorine (FAC) in the wash water, with typical practice in fresh-cut produce operations using 100–150 ppm FAC. At this concentration, the chlorinated wash kills surface pathogens on vegetables and fruit and a potable-water rinse afterwards keeps residual chlorine low (follow the residue limits of the local food-safety authority). The wash solution should be held at pH 6.5–7.5, where half or more of the free chlorine is hypochlorous acid (HOCl), the fast-acting form — at pH 8 only about a quarter is HOCl and the rest is the much weaker hypochlorite ion (OCl⁻), so the wash kills far more slowly. In Oman's hot climate, produce temperatures can be high, which accelerates chlorine degradation and requires more frequent solution replacement. Global Chemicals LLC supplies food-grade sodium hypochlorite with test strips and photometric kits for accurate FAC monitoring in food operations.

title: Urea (Food/Feed Grade)
description: Non-protein nitrogen source for ruminant feed, with narrow food and fermentation uses.

details.longDescription:
Urea (carbamide, CH4N2O, CAS 57-13-6) is listed here as food/feed grade: white crystalline prills of 99% minimum purity containing 46% nitrogen, with biuret below 1%, in 50 kg bags or bulk. Most of it goes to feed mills, dairy and livestock farms and makers of feed blocks; its use in food and fermentation is much narrower.

In ruminant feed for cattle, sheep and goats, urea is a non-protein nitrogen (NPN) source: rumen microbes break it down to ammonia and use that to build microbial protein, provided the ration also supplies fermentable energy and sulphur. It goes into concentrates and total mixed rations and molasses-urea blocks and licks, and is used to raise the crude protein of silage and to treat straw. It has to be mixed evenly and introduced gradually, and the usual limits are about 1% of total diet dry matter or 3% of the concentrate. Overfeeding, poor mixing or animals gorging on it cause ammonia poisoning, which can kill within hours. Pigs, poultry and other non-ruminants cannot use it as a protein source. All of this is animal feed, not human food.

Its uses in human food are limited. In the European Union it is authorised as the food additive E927b only in chewing gum without added sugar, and it is used as a nitrogen source for yeast in industrial fermentation, for example fuel-ethanol production. It has largely been dropped from winemaking because it leads to ethyl carbamate in the wine. Food-processing buyers should check that the specification meets the additive rules of the market they sell into before ordering. Agricultural urea for date palms, vegetables and cereals is listed separately as Urea 46% N Fertilizer, in 25 kg bags and 1,000 kg big bags; this listing is the feed and process grade.

Handling and storage: urea is not classified as hazardous under GHS by most suppliers and is not regulated for transport. It is hygroscopic and very soluble, about 108 g in 100 mL of water at 20 °C, so damp prills cake; keep bags closed, dry, shaded and off the floor. Keep it away from strong oxidisers, from nitric acid, with which it forms explosive urea nitrate, and from sodium or calcium hypochlorite and other chlorine products, with which it can form explosive nitrogen trichloride. Heating releases ammonia. Store feed-grade stock apart from fertilisers and other chemicals to avoid mix-ups and contamination, and wear gloves and goggles when handling it in quantity.

It is supplied in 50 kg bags and in bulk, with same-day delivery in Muscat, next-day delivery to Sohar, two to three days to Salalah, and export across the GCC. A safety data sheet comes with it and a certificate of analysis is available on request; send the quantity and intended use for a quote.

technicalSpecs: Safe feeding level: ~1% of total diet DM or 3% of concentrate (ruminants)

title: White Salt (Food Grade)
description: Food-grade refined sodium chloride for seasoning and preservation.

details.longDescription:
Food-grade white salt (refined sodium chloride, NaCl, CAS 7647-14-5) is supplied by Global Chemicals LLC at 99.5% minimum purity with heavy metals below 10 ppm, as clean white crystalline granules in fine, medium and coarse grain sizes, iodised or non-iodised, in 1 kg, 25 kg and 50 kg bags from stock in Muscat to food manufacturers, meat and fish processors, bakeries, dairies, restaurants and catering companies across Oman. Each lot ships with a certificate of analysis and the food-safety documentation buyers need for their own audits; the laboratory reagent and industrial grades are listed separately.

Which grain to order. Fine salt dissolves fastest and is the seasoning and bakery salt, dosed at about 1.8–2.2% of flour weight in bread, where it controls fermentation and strengthens gluten as well as seasoning the loaf. Medium grain is the general processing salt for soups, sauces, snacks and ready meals. Coarse salt is for brines, pickling, curing, fish salting and cheese making, where slow dissolution and even coverage matter; cheese makers salt curds or brine wheels with it, and meat processors build curing brines from it with the nitrite cure added separately. Fermentation of vegetables, olives and sauces uses the non-iodised grade, because iodine can inhibit the culture and darken the product. Iodised salt carries the standard iodine fortification for table and household use.

Why refined: raw sea salt carries magnesium and calcium chlorides that make it bitter and hygroscopic, plus sand and organic matter; refining removes them, which is what gives this salt its clean taste, white colour, free flow and consistent brine strength.

Storage and handling: salt is not hazardous, but it is corrosive to mild steel and absorbs moisture in humid air, so keep bags closed, dry and off the floor, use plastic or stainless equipment for brines, and rotate stock. It is non-perishable.

Delivery is same day within Muscat, next day to Sohar, two to three days to Salalah and Duqm, and by road to the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain with a certificate of origin. Request a quote with the grain size, iodised or not, bag size and monthly volume.
